newsitem.title: UK: Tory chief says UK govt petulant and sanctimonious.
newsitem.headline: Tory chief says UK govt petulant and sanctimonious.

text.p: Britain's new Conservative Party leader William Hague, in bullish mood after a by-election victory, has accused the Labour government of being petulant and sanctimonious.
In a sharp weekend attack on Prime Minister Tony Blair, he said: "There is a high-handedness and intolerance in this government."

The 36-year-old Hague, elected Conservative leader after his party was crushed by Labour in general elections three months ago following 18 years in power, insisted the badly bruised Tories were fighting back.
Parliament has now gone into summer recess with Labour enjoying a massive majority of 178 seats in the 659-seat lower chamber.
But that did not discourage Hague from launching a furious broadside against Blair's first 100 days in power.
"They have developed a sanctimoniousness and a self-righteousness which makes it hard for them to see where they are going wrong," he told The Sunday Telegraph.
"In the end there is always a penalty to be paid for being a control freak in politics and that is what they have become."
Hague accused Blair of "acting petulantly" in parliament when queried over the appointment of former businessman Lord David Simon as Minister for Trade and Competitiveness in Europe.
He pressed the prime minister on why Simon, the former chairman of British Petroleum Plc, did not sell shares worth two million pounds ($3.3 million) in the company when he took up the post.

In the first test of voter opinion since the May 1 election, Conservative candidate John Randall secured a five percent swing away from Labour to retain the west London seat of Uxbridge in a parliamentary by-election last week.
Hague, launching salvoes against Blair in the weekend media, said: "The Conservative Party is back in business."
Writing in Sunday's tabloid News of the World, he admitted that the Conservatives had been drummed out of office because "millions of voters came to see us as divided, sleazy and arrogant."
Hague pledged that a new-look Conservative Party under him would be united, democratic and open. He promised it would name its major benefactors and refuse to accept donations from abroad.
The surprise victory in Uxbridge came despite recent opinion polls showing that Labour had 57 percent of voter support nationwide compared to just 23 percent for the Conservatives.
